+# ADR 0001: Increase Pricing Cache TTL from 900 to 3600 Seconds
+
+## Status
+
+Accepted
+
+## Context
+
+Our pricing service currently caches pricing data with a time-to-live (TTL) of 900 seconds (15 minutes). This relatively short TTL was initially chosen to ensure pricing information remained current while balancing cache efficiency. However, analysis of our pricing update patterns has shown that pricing changes are infrequent events, typically occurring during scheduled maintenance windows or promotional campaigns rather than continuously throughout the day. The 15-minute TTL results in excessive cache misses and redundant database queries during normal operation, increasing load on our pricing service and degrading response times during peak traffic periods.
+
+Additionally, our infrastructure monitoring indicates that pricing data stability is high, with updates rarely occurring more than a few times per day. The cost of stale pricing data (15 minutes old) is negligible compared to the operational benefits of reduced database load. Our pricing contract with clients specifies a maximum freshness requirement of 1 hour, providing explicit headroom for cache decisions.
+
+## Decision
+
+We have decided to increase the pricing cache TTL from 900 seconds to 3600 seconds (1 hour). This change will apply to all pricing-related caches throughout the system, including tier-based pricing, promotional pricing, and regional pricing variants. The cache invalidation strategy remains event-driven; cache entries will continue to be invalidated immediately when pricing data is updated through administrative channels, ensuring that critical updates propagate instantly despite the longer TTL.
+
+To mitigate risks, we will implement cache refresh logic that proactively warms the cache for popular pricing tiers before their TTL expires, reducing the likelihood of cache misses during traffic spikes. Monitoring will be enhanced to track cache hit rates, database query counts, and pricing freshness metrics to validate the benefits of this change.
+
+## Consequences
+
+The increased TTL will significantly reduce database query volume during normal operation, resulting in lower infrastructure costs and improved response latencies for pricing lookups. Cache hit rates are expected to increase from approximately 60% to 90%, with corresponding reductions in database load. This will free up capacity on our pricing service to handle peak traffic more gracefully and reduce the likelihood of cascading failures during traffic spikes.
+
+The trade-off is that pricing data may be up to 1 hour stale during normal cache lifetime. While event-driven invalidation mitigates this for most updates, urgent pricing corrections will take at most 1 hour to propagate if the cache is not explicitly invalidated. This aligns with our service-level agreements and is acceptable given the performance gains. We will establish monitoring alerts to flag any pricing updates that occur without corresponding cache invalidations, helping us maintain correctness over time.
